topic: The illusion of transparency: others can't read you as well as you think
title: The Illusion of Transparency: Can People Read You?
voiceover: Can other people really read how you feel? In 1998, Thomas Gilovich, Kenneth Savitsky and Victoria Medvec published research on the illusion of transparency. It's the tendency to overestimate how well others can read your emotional states. In one experiment, Cornell students told lies. Observers then watched each student and judged whether that student was lying. About half of the liars thought they had been caught. But only about a quarter actually were. So the liars overestimated how transparent they were. This was a laboratory study with students, not every real-world situation, so treat it as one data point. So in this research, people were less readable than they feared. Tomorrow: is there a real research difference between narcissism and confidence?

description: Do others see your nervousness? In a classic study, about half of liars thought they had been caught, but only about a quarter actually were. Psychologists call this the illusion of transparency. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Gilovich, T., Savitsky, K., & Medvec, V. H. (1998). The illusion of transparency: Biased assessments of others' ability to read one's emotional states. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(2), 332-346.
accuracy_note: The liar figures (about half vs about a quarter) come from secondary summaries of one experiment in Gilovich, Savitsky & Medvec (1998). The sample was Cornell students; results may differ elsewhere.
